Let me start by understanding the situation better. First, I'm a first-year associate at a local firm, and my senior associate has been there for three years. A few weeks ago, I wasn't feeling well and threw up right after waking up. I notified her that I wouldn't be coming to work because I was sick. She seemed disappointed but allowed me to take a sick leave. That's good because she understood that I was unwell. On that day, I sent a few emails to our client as she had requested the previous day and tried to get some sleep. But while I was trying to rest, she kept texting me with things I needed to do. I tried to ignore the messages and turned off my phone's notifications to get some sleep. After about an hour, she called me and told me that I had to send her a file immediately regarding the client's data, which she didn't have on her laptop. I sent her the files and asked if she needed anything else since I was going to the doctor and wouldn't bring my laptop with me. She said that was all for now. I went to the doctor, who told me I was overworked because I had been working overtime until 2-3 AM for the past two months and needed some rest. On my way home, my senior associate texted me again, asking me to get our client's billing information, something she could have done herself since she has their contacts. I did as she asked and forwarded her the information. When I got home, I took the prescribed medicine and fell asleep. I was shocked when I woke up to find my phone with two missed calls and 30 new messages from her, giving me work to do from home. I felt it was a bit unfair of her to give me work while I was on sick leave, so I ignored the messages and didn't reply. Now, the question is: Is it right or wrong for me to ignore her texts? I need to think about this carefully. First, I should consider the expectations in the workplace regarding sick leave. Typically, when someone is on sick leave, they are expected to rest and recover. However, depending on the company's culture and policies, there might be different expectations about being available to handle work-related matters, even while sick. In this case, my senior associate kept texting me with work-related tasks, even after I had informed her that I was sick and wouldn't be bringing my laptop home. She asked for files and information that she could have potentially handled herself, especially since she has the client's contacts. This makes me feel that she was overstepping by expecting me to continue working while I was unwell. Moreover, the fact that I had been working overtime for the past two months and was advised by the doctor to rest suggests that I needed that time off to recover both physically and mentally. Ignoring her texts allowed me to focus on my health and well-being, which is important. On the other hand, ignoring her texts might have come across as unprofessional or disrespectful, especially since she is a senior associate and has been with the firm longer than I have. It's possible that she expected me to be more responsive, even while on sick leave. I also need to consider the potential consequences of ignoring her texts. If she feels that I was not cooperative or that I didn't take my responsibilities seriously, it could affect our working relationship. However, given the circumstances—my illness, the overwork, and the doctor's advice—it seems justified to prioritize my health over responding to work-related messages. Additionally, I should think about whether there was a better way to handle the situation. Perhaps instead of ignoring the messages, I could have sent a brief reply explaining that I was unwell and would be unable to handle work-related tasks at that time. This would have communicated my situation clearly while maintaining professionalism. In conclusion, while ignoring her texts might have been seen as wrong in some contexts, given the specific circumstances of my illness, overwork, and the doctor's advice, it was a reasonable decision to prioritize my health and well-being. However, finding a balance by communicating my situation could have been a better approach to maintain professional relationships.
